Compositional data (CoDa) model of life-table deaths

Source: R/model-coda.R
coda.Rd

coda() is the Lee-Carter model in compositional form (Oeppen 2008), as formulated by Bergeron-Boucher, Canudas-Romo, Oeppen and Vaupel (2017). It models the life-table distribution of deaths by age (which sums to 1). With coherent = TRUE or common_by, it is their coherent model for several populations. The code follows the reference implementation, model.Oeppen() and model.OeppenC() of the R package MortalityForecast 0.8.1 (Pascariu and Bergeron-Boucher), and reproduces its fitted values and point forecasts.

Usage

coda(jump_off = c("observed", "fitted"), coherent = FALSE, common_by = NULL)

Arguments

jump_off

"observed" (forecasts start from the observed deaths of the last year) or "fitted" (from the fitted deaths).

coherent

Fit the coherent model with a common component per group.

common_by

Stratum variable(s) defining groups with their own common component (implies coherent = TRUE); NULL with coherent = TRUE puts all strata in one group.

Value

A model specification.

Details

The model of one stratum has six steps:

  1. the death rates of each year give life-table deaths d[x, t] with radix 1 at the first age (life_table() conventions); for a closed age range, the survivors at its upper bound are an extra part, so that the parts sum to 1;

  2. a[x] is the geometric mean of d[x, t] over the years, closed to 1;

  3. the deaths are centred by perturbation (d[x, t] / a[x], closed) and transformed by the centred log-ratio (clr);

  4. the first component of a singular value decomposition gives clr(d[x, t] / a[x]) = b[x] k[t] (b sums to zero);

  5. k[t] follows a random walk with drift (ARIMA(0,1,0) with drift, the default of the reference implementation);

  6. forecasts are transformed back (inverse clr, perturbation by a, closure) to life-table deaths and then to death rates.

With jump_off = "observed" (the default, as jumpchoice = "actual" of the reference implementation), forecasts are the observed deaths of the last year T perturbed by the change of the model: d[x, T + j] is proportional to d_obs[x, T] exp(b[x] (k[T + j] - k[T])). With "fitted", forecasts start from the fitted deaths of the last year. The forecast of year T + j uses the index j steps ahead; the reference implementation uses j + 1 steps, which makes no difference for the observed jump-off with a random walk with drift.

Coherent model. With coherent = TRUE or common_by (for example "sex"), the strata of each group (all strata, or each level of common_by) share a common component (Bergeron-Boucher et al. 2017): clr(d[x, t, i] / a[x, i]) = B[x] K[t] + b[x, i] k[t, i]. The common component B K is the first component of the CoDa model of the average distribution of the group, the closed geometric mean of the life-table deaths of its strata (the centre of the compositions). The deviations of each stratum are the first component of the remaining variation. K follows a random walk with drift, and k[t, i] an AR(1) process with mean (estimated by maximum likelihood), as in the reference implementation (model.OeppenC(), defaults order.B = c(0, 1, 0) with drift and order.D = c(1, 0, 0) without drift), so the deviations stay bounded. If the data carry a hierarchy (see mt_aggregate_strata()), the average uses the bottom strata only, as li_lee() does.

Open age interval. Life-table deaths of an open interval are the survivors at its lower bound; they do not determine its death rate, and the reference implementation forecasts the deaths only. Here the log death rate of the open interval gets loadings on the same indexes, estimated by least squares: log m[open, t] = a_o + b_o k[t], and in the coherent model log m[open, t, i] = a_o[i] + B_o K[t] + b_o[i] k[t, i], with B_o from the mean log rate of the group. The open interval thus follows the rest of the age pattern (and the jump-off rule). An auxiliary random walk on the observed log rate, as in tucker3(), accumulates the noise of the few deaths at the highest ages: on French data (ages 100+, forecasts of 10 years) a quarter to a half of its paths exceeded a rate of 1.

Zero deaths. Cells with zero deaths have no logarithm. As replace.zeros() of the reference implementation (method "min"), zero rates are replaced by half the smallest positive rate of the stratum in the training years; a warning is given when more than 10% of the cells are affected.

Draws simulate the indexes: the random walk with drift includes the uncertainty of the drift (normal, with the variance of the mean change), the AR(1) processes their innovations; a and b are fixed. Draws are expected rates; predictive draws (mt_forecast(predictive = TRUE)) add Poisson variation of the deaths given the rates and the exposures, and no other observation noise. If intervals are too narrow on real data, that is a property of the model (see recalibrated(), ensemble(), or overdispersed models such as stanmomo(family = "nb")). The model weights all ages equally on the clr scale, so the noise of ages with few deaths enters k; its intervals can be wider than those of lee_carter().

References

Oeppen J (2008). Coherent forecasting of multiple-decrement life tables: a test using Japanese cause of death data. CODAWORK'08, Universitat de Girona.

Bergeron-Boucher M-P, Canudas-Romo V, Oeppen J, Vaupel JW (2017). Coherent forecasts of mortality with compositional data analysis. Demographic Research 37(17): 527-566. doi:10.4054/DemRes.2017.37.17

See also

coda_causes() for causes of death, lee_carter() for the model of death rates, li_lee() for its coherent version.

Examples

x <- mt_example(deaths = "single", years = 1995:2012)
fc <- mt_forecast(mt_fit(coda(), x), h = 5, n_draws = 50, seed = 1)
fc2 <- mt_forecast(mt_fit(coda(coherent = TRUE), x), h = 5, n_draws = 50, seed = 1)
